quiz.0.question: In advanced food pairing, what effect does food 'sweetness' have on wine?
quiz.0.options.1: Makes the wine taste drier, more bitter and less fruity — the wine appears to lose its sweetness
quiz.0.options.2: Has no effect on the wine's perceived sweetness
quiz.0.explanation: Sweet food reduces the perceived sweetness of the wine — a dry wine beside a sweet dish tastes austere, thin and bitter. The wine must match or exceed the sweetness of the food.
quiz.1.question: When facing a rich, fatty dish (fried seafood, creamy risotto), what is the best 'contrasting pairing' strategy?
quiz.1.options.0: Pair with a heavy, tannic red wine
quiz.1.options.1: Pair with a high-acid wine (Prosecco, Verdicchio, Gavi) — the acidity cuts through the fat
quiz.1.options.3: Avoid pairing — fatty food doesn't need wine
quiz.1.explanation: The classic contrasting principle: high acidity provides contrast to rich fat — cutting through the richness and refreshing the palate. This is why Champagne with fried food works so brilliantly.
quiz.2.question: Umami-rich food makes wine more bitter. But if the umami dish also has strong SALTINESS (Parmigiano, prosciutto), how should you pair?
quiz.2.options.0: Avoid wine with salty umami food
quiz.2.options.1: Saltiness counteracts the negative effect of umami on wine — moderately salty umami dishes become much more wine-friendly
quiz.2.options.2: Pair with very sweet wine to counter the saltiness
quiz.2.explanation: Saltiness suppresses bitterness (including umami-induced bitterness in wine). Salty-umami dishes (aged Parmigiano, prosciutto crudo) are far more wine-friendly than pure umami — the salt corrects the wine-pairing problem.
quiz.3.question: Which pairing best represents the 'regional pairing' philosophy — 'what grows together, goes together'?
quiz.3.options.1: Chianti Classico with Florentine bistecca or ribollita (Tuscany)
quiz.3.options.3: Vermentino with a Piemontese truffle dish
quiz.3.explanation: Regional pairing means pairing within the same wine and food traditions — Chianti Classico and Florentine cuisine evolved together over centuries. The tannic, acidic Sangiovese perfectly suits the fatty, herb-rich Tuscan cuisine.
